meta.tagline: A megacity of a thousand minarets in the shadow of the pyramids

overview.title: Welcome to Cairo
overview.intro: Cairo doesn't meet you halfway; it embraces you, shakes you, and never quite lets go. In this megacity of twenty million the horn symphony never rests — yet in the same city a felucca glides silently on the Nile, thousand-year-old minarets glow along El-Muizz Street, and on the horizon's edge the pyramids have waited in the same spot for four and a half millennia. The bazaar seller of Khan el-Khalili, the mint-tea man at the ahwa, the master at the koshary counter — they all say the same sentence: 'Welcome to Egypt!' Surrender to its chaos but know its rules; to the prepared traveler, Cairo is one of the world's most generous cities.

local_word.definition: Egypt's magic word: 'never mind, it happens, don't worry' all in one. Traffic gridlocked? Maalesh. Plans changed? Maalesh. It's not a shrug but a philosophy of life — the locals found the key to staying calm in Cairo's chaos thousands of years ago.

rules.title: Go to the pyramids at the first hour
rules.description: Be inside the moment the Giza gates open: the light is soft, the heat merciful, the crowds and hustlers still thin. Toward noon both the sun and the commotion multiply. The site is vast — bring water, wear real shoes, allow three to four hours.

rules.title: Use ride apps in the city
rules.description: In classic taxis the meter is usually 'broken' and the haggling is exhausting: Uber and Careem are cheap, everywhere and painless in Cairo. The price is fixed up front and no address explanations are needed — the traffic is adventure enough; the payment shouldn't be.

rules.title: Learn to say no with a smile
rules.description: 'La shukran' (no, thank you) is your most valuable sentence in Cairo: everything extended like a gift is a sale, every favor may expect baksheesh. Don't get angry — smile and keep walking. The tourist who draws the line clearly sees Cairo's best face.

quick_facts.label: Signature
quick_facts.sub: At the city's edge — even the metro gets close

quick_facts.label: Currency
quick_facts.sub: Cash is king; stock small notes

tip.label: The Cairo philosophy
tip.text: In this city the plan should be flexible, the stomach sturdy and the humor ready: one 'maalesh' and a smile beat a hundred frustrations. Pick one big goal per day and leave the rest to Cairo's current — the city will impose its own program anyway.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Cairo traffic is legendary; the antidotes are ride apps, the metro and the Nile itself — walk the short distances, choose the long ones wisely.

items.title: Arriving from the airport
items.description: Cairo Airport is 45–60 minutes from the center depending on traffic: the cleanest solution is Uber/Careem or a hotel transfer. Smile past the 'taxi my friend' chorus at the door — the app price is a third of theirs.

items.title: Uber and Careem
items.description: The city's real public transport: cheap, ubiquitous, haggle-free. Take the time estimates seriously in traffic, but leave the route to the driver — a Cairo driver knows alleys the navigation has never heard of.

items.title: The metro
items.description: Three lines leap over the traffic: key stops like Sadat (Tahrir) and Mar Girgis (Coptic Cairo) are gold for visitors too. There are women-only cars — a comfortable option for women travelers at rush hour.

items.title: A felucca on the Nile
items.description: An hour on the Nile under sail: no motor, no horns, just canvas in the wind. Hire before sunset and settle the price before boarding — the most graceful revenge available on the city's noise.

items.title: Walking within districts
items.description: Cairo as a whole can't be walked, but its districts can: El-Muizz Street, the lanes of Zamalek, the courtyards of Coptic Cairo. Crossing the street is an art form — sidle up to a local and cross in their slipstream.

callout.label: Traffic tip
callout.text: Friday morning is the only moment Cairo sleeps: roads empty, air clear, the pyramids and El-Muizz calm. Put long-distance plans on Friday morning and museums on weekdays — after Friday noon prayers the city boils again.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Cairo choosing a district means choosing your comfort level: the green of the Nile island, the loud grandeur of downtown, or Giza with a pyramid view.

local_word.definition: The doorman-guard-messenger who lives at the entrance of every building: the invisible manager of Cairo's social life. He takes the packages, appraises the visitors, and knows every piece of neighborhood news. If you rent a flat, greet your bawab — he's your most valuable ally in the city.

items.name: Zamalek
items.description: The island district in the middle of the Nile: tree-lined streets, embassies, cafes and galleries. Cairo's intensity turned down one notch — the softest landing for a first visit.

items.name: Downtown (Wust el-Balad)
items.description: Belle époque boulevards within walking distance of Tahrir and the museum: loud, exhausting, unforgettable. Historic coffeehouses and nightlife at the doorstep — for those who want Cairo unfiltered.

items.name: Garden City
items.description: The old diplomatic quarter of curving streets just south of downtown: near the center but one street removed from the horn symphony. The Nile-side hotels line this strip too.

items.name: Giza — pyramid view
items.description: Hotels with pyramid-view terraces: open the curtains and Khufu greets you. Far from the center — but if your program leans on the pyramids and Saqqara, a legendary choice for a night or two.

items.name: Maadi
items.description: The leafy southern district beloved of long-term expats: cafes, Nile walks, a metro link. For staying in Cairo as if you lived there — the center is twenty minutes by metro.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Cairo's calendar is a negotiation with the desert sun: October to April is the golden window; summer is a city of early mornings and late evenings.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Desert Spring
items.subtitle: Spring · Mild days, the occasional sand wind
items.description: March and April bring mild days and cool nights: a comfortable season for the pyramids and open-air plans. The sand wind called khamsin occasionally yellows the sky — that day is a museum day, maalesh.

callout.label: April tip
callout.text: On an April morning the light at Giza is a photographer's friend and the noon heat still merciful. If your dates hit Sham el-Nessim, the spring holiday, the parks turn into one great picnic — you'll see Cairenes on their most cheerful day.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Bargaining with the Heat
items.subtitle: Summer · Scorching noons, vivid nights
items.description: Days reach 35–40°C: the program splits into 07:00–11:00 and after 17:00. In exchange, hotels get cheaper and Cairo nights return to their true character — at midnight the city is queueing for ice cream.

callout.label: Midday note
callout.text: Insisting on open-air sightseeing at summer noon drains the body: give 11:00–17:00 to air-conditioned museums, ahwa breaks and the hotel pool. The water bottle and hat are non-negotiable.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The Golden Window Opens
items.subtitle: Autumn · Softening sun, ideal touring weather
items.description: With October the heat relents: pyramid mornings are cool and Nile evenings silken. High season begins, but December's crowds are still far — this is Cairo's most balanced touring window.

callout.label: November tip
callout.text: In November the sun sets early: book your felucca for the 16:00–17:00 band and catch the golden hour on the water. It's also the year's most comfortable month for Saqqara and Dahshur — the desert wind blows cool.

items.label: Winter
items.name: The Crown of High Season
items.subtitle: Winter · Cool sunny days, crowded sites
items.description: Days are sunny at 18–22°C and nights ask for a cardigan: perfect touring weather. The world knows it too — the pyramids and museums are at their year's busiest and prices peak. Early booking and a morning strategy are essential.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: In winter crowds, reverse the usual order: enter the pyramids at gate opening and visit the great museum in the afternoon — tour groups flow museum-first, pyramids-at-noon; flow the other way and you'll see both in peace.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: The Egyptian table is the people's kitchen: the generosity of the stew pot, the reign of the legume, and the speed of the street cart — all at once.

local_word.definition: It means both coffee and coffeehouse: the salon of Cairo's social life, with bubbling shisha, clacking backgammon and mint-tea steam. Nobody hurries at an ahwa; the tea glass shrinks, the conversation grows. Order 'ahwa mazbut' and you get medium-sweet coffee brewed the Turkish way — it will taste familiar.

items.name: Koshary
items.description: Rice, pasta, lentils, chickpeas, fried onions and spiced tomato sauce in one bowl: Egypt's national fast food. Served at the counter to a percussion of spoons — top with garlic vinegar (dakka) and hot sauce, to the limit of your courage.
items.tag: The national bowl · dakka to your courage

items.name: Ful and ta'meya breakfast
items.description: Ful, the slow-stewed fava mash, and ta'meya, Egypt's green-hearted falafel made from fava beans: rolled into baladi bread, crowned with pickles. Hot off the street cart in the morning — this is how Cairo starts its day.

items.name: Molokhia
items.description: A garlicky, coriander-scented soup-sauce of finely chopped jute leaves: with chicken or rabbit, over rice. The texture plays tricks on newcomers, the flavor becomes an addiction — try it at a home-cooking eatery.

items.name: The grill and mahshi table
items.description: Kofta, chicken skewers and charcoal meat; alongside, rice-stuffed mahshi vegetables and tahini. The kebab table is laid with an army of salads and pickles — the baladi bread keeps arriving hot.

items.name: Feteer
items.description: Egypt's layered butter pastry: savory with cheese or meat, sweet with honey and cream. The baker spinning the dough in the air is half the show — order it hot from the stone oven.
items.tag: Layered and buttery · hot from the oven

items.name: Om Ali and the juice stand
items.description: Om Ali, the baked bread pudding with milk, nuts and raisins, is eaten hot; alongside, a street glass of fresh-pressed sugarcane juice (asab). A sweet craving never goes unanswered in Cairo.
items.tag: Hot dessert + asab · the street duo

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: Good food in Cairo is astonishingly cheap: wherever you see a tourist menu, the price has tripled. A koshary counter with a queue, a full home-cooking eatery and a busy street bakery never mislead — and for water, always sealed bottles, everywhere.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees the pyramids and the great museum; these six are the hidden doors into Cairo's layers.

items.name: Al-Azhar Park
items.description: A park reclaimed from an old rubbish hill, facing historic Cairo's thousand-minaret skyline: at sunset the Muhammad Ali Mosque turns to gold. Sit in the tea garden and listen to the call-to-prayer symphony from above — the city's most peaceful hour.

items.name: El-Muizz Street by night
items.description: The main street of Fatimid Cairo opens differently under evening lights: madrasas, sabils and caravanserais glow honey-colored. The crowds thin and the stonework takes the stage — even if you saw it by day, return at night.

items.rarity: Reading the city from a minaret
items.name: Bab Zuweila
items.description: You can climb the minarets of the Fatimid walls' southern gate: the rooftops, laundry lines and minaret forest of historic Cairo lie at your feet. Modest entrance, generous view — and the tentmakers' bazaar is right at the gate.

items.name: Coptic Cairo (Mar Girgis)
items.description: The Hanging Church, the crypt of St. Sergius and the Ben Ezra Synagogue in one labyrinth of courtyards: an island of silence built into Roman towers. Reached by metro — Cairo's calmest half day is here.

items.name: Tanoura at Wekalet El Ghouri
items.description: On set evenings, the courtyard of a Mameluke caravanserai hosts the tanoura (whirling) performance: rainbow skirts spin for hours and the rhythm becomes a trance. The ticket is modest, the atmosphere spellbinding — go early, the courtyard is small.

items.rarity: Palace garden on a Nile island
items.name: Manial Palace
items.description: A prince's palace on Roda Island: Ottoman, Moorish and Art Nouveau styles under one roof, wrapped in a tropical garden. Skipped by the crowds, this mansion is a quiet window onto the last era of Cairo's aristocracy.

callout.label: Layer strategy
callout.text: Don't try to 'finish' Cairo in one pass: the pharaonic layer (Giza + museum), the Islamic layer (El-Muizz + the Citadel), the Coptic layer (Mar Girgis) and the Nile layer (felucca + Zamalek) each want their own half day. Always slot an ahwa break between them — the city makes sense during the breaks.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Cairo's games are ancient and the script never changes; the tourist who knows the lines stays friends with the city.

items.name: The pyramid 'gift' and camel game
items.description: The headscarf extended 'for free', the volunteer who 'takes your photo', the camel that's 'free to mount': all are invoiced on the way down. Mounting a camel is easy; dismounting is a negotiation.
items.instead: Take nothing from anyone's hand — say 'la shukran' and walk. If you want a camel or horse, fix the price, duration and dismount point before mounting; pay no one outside the official ticket office.

items.name: The 'museum is closed today' script
items.description: A 'helpful' stranger appears at the gate: 'This is closed until noon, let me take you somewhere lovely' — the route always ends at a cousin's perfume or papyrus shop.
items.instead: Check opening hours yourself and walk to the ticket window: unless the person saying 'closed' is the ticket clerk, smile and pass. Official tickets always come from the gate or the official online channel.

items.name: Shops dressed as 'government stores'
items.description: Most perfume, papyrus and spice shops signed 'government shop' or 'fixed price museum store' are private businesses: prices are free-form, the stories rich. 'Papyrus' printed on banana leaf is a bonus.
items.instead: Accept the haggle from the start for souvenirs: open at a third of the first price and bargain with a smile. Real papyrus doesn't crack when folded — ask for the test; for quality work, choose a shop that shows you its workshop.

items.name: Baksheesh ambiguity
items.description: At the toilet door, from the guard offering to 'open a hidden tomb', for the photo taken unasked: the palm is always open and your change can 'disappear'.
items.instead: Carry plenty of small notes: a small tip for a small service is normal, and you set the number. Cut off 'let me show you a special place' offers at the door — the tourist who enters a forbidden area pays a bigger fine than the guard.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: Anger doesn't work in Cairo; humor opens every door: treat haggling as a game, memorize 'la shukran', never withhold a smile. The traveler who draws clear lines yet stays friendly leaves this city with stories and friends.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From pharaoh to felucca — a megacity day

steps.title: Giza morning
steps.description: Be at the foot of the pyramids at gate opening: see Khufu's scale and the Sphinx's gaze in morning light. Walk out to the panorama point — water in hand.

steps.title: Ful and ta'meya break
steps.description: A late street-cart breakfast on the way back: ta'meya in baladi bread, tea alongside. Cheap, hot, true.

steps.title: Great museum hours
steps.description: Allow three hours for Tutankhamun's treasure and the pharaonic halls: crowds thin in the afternoon. The air conditioning is a bonus.

steps.title: Khan el-Khalili and El-Muizz
steps.description: Haggling practice in the bazaar's side lanes, then the stonework of El-Muizz: be there as the evening lights come on.

steps.title: Ahwa break at El-Fishawy
steps.description: Mint tea in the centuries-old mirrored coffeehouse: Nobel laureate Naguib Mahfouz kept a table here. Shisha bubbling in the background.

steps.title: Felucca finale on the Nile
steps.description: Sail out after sunset: the city's lights on the water, the horns far away. A reconciliation session with Cairo — then dinner in Zamalek.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Pyramids, minarets and the Nile — Cairo layer by layer

steps.title: Classic Cairo
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: Giza morning, the museum, Khan el-Khalili, El-Muizz, ahwa, felucca.

steps.title: Islamic Cairo in depth
steps.description: Morning at the Citadel and the Muhammad Ali Mosque; noon in the colossal courtyard of the Sultan Hassan Madrasa; afternoon up the Bab Zuweila minaret and through the tentmakers' bazaar; sunset at Al-Azhar Park + the tanoura show at Wekalet El Ghouri.

steps.title: Saqqara, Coptic Cairo and farewell
steps.description: Morning at Saqqara's Step Pyramid and Dahshur's Red Pyramid (go inside!); noon in the courtyards of Coptic Cairo at Mar Girgis; afternoon of cafes and galleries in Zamalek; farewell dinner at a koshary master — extra dakka.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Egyptian Arabic is warm and witty; these five phrases open doors in the bazaar, at the table and on the street.

items.meaning: The foundation of greeting — say it entering a shop; 'aleykum salam' comes back
Thank you — and 'la shukran' is the polite no; your most-used sentence
How much? — the opening move of the haggle; don't forget to smile at the answer
Never mind, don't worry — Cairo's philosophy of life in one word
Let's go! — you'll hear it a hundred times a day in Cairo

checklist.title: Cairo Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Yalla! You've lived the city of a thousand minarets the way it deserves!
